The organic kale was luminous under the misters. A fine, artificial rain. Leo’s hand hovered, the fingers trembling. He hadn’t slept in three days. The jagged scar on his forearm, a pink lightning bolt from the crash debris, itched under his sleeve. He couldn’t remember what he came for. Milk? No. The list was in his other hand, a crumpled, damp thing. He stared at the vegetables, the bright green, the wet…

And then the refrigeration unit kicked in. A low, resonant hum ascended from the floor, vibrating through the waxed linoleum and into the soles of his boots. It wasn’t a fridge. It was a rotor. The twin GE T700s on a Black Hawk spooling up. The air changed. It thickened, became heavy with the phantom scent of JP-8 jet fuel. The smell is so corrosive, so real, it burns the back of his throat. He’s not in the produce aisle. He’s in the bird. The bird is going down. The world is a brutal, shaking machine of shrieking metal.

A woman reaches past him for a head of lettuce. Her arm in his peripheral vision is a blur of motion, a muzzle flash. He flinches so hard his shoulder pops. The kale tumbles. The crash is happening now. The altimeter is a blur of spinning numbers. Mikey, the door gunner, is strapped in across from him, his mouth open in a silent scream that Leo can’t hear over the screaming engine. The whole fuselage is a blender. Mikey’s eyes are locked on Leo’s, wide and terrified, a sudden, shocking intimacy before the world tilts. The ceiling is the floor. The floor is the sky. Leo’s stomach is in his throat. The impact is a wall of oblivion. A wet, percussive thud. And then silence. Just the tick-tick-tick of a dying engine and the drip of something hot and wet. Leo’s back in the grocery store, on his knees, gasping, his heart a frantic, trapped bird against his ribs. Someone is asking if he’s okay. He can’t answer. Mikey’s face is still there, burned onto his retinas, a silent, eternal accusation. He was the only one to walk away. The guilt is a physical weight, a stone in his chest, heavier than the rotor wash.

Standing in her house this morning, I could still smell her. Not just the perfume on the dresser, but the scent of her kitchen on a Sunday morning—coffee, cinnamon, and unconditional love. For me, she wasn't just a grandmother; she was my true north, the steady star that my entire sky turned around. And now that star has gone out, and the world feels terrifyingly dark and directionless. I feel completely untethered.

I was there, holding her hand, counting her breaths as if my own will could make each one last an hour. And when the last one came, a soft, rattling sigh, it wasn't just a sound. It was the world shifting. The silence that followed wasn't peaceful; it was a deafening, hollow void where her voice used to be.

But I refuse to let that silence be the final word. Because her life was not a whisper. It was a song. She taught me how to find beauty in the simplest things, how to be strong enough to be gentle, and how to love without holding anything back. Her hands, which held mine when I was a scared child, were the safest place in the world. She built a home not just with walls and a roof, but with her spirit.

I carry a crushing pain in my chest right now, a physical ache that makes it hard to breathe. But I realize that this pain is just all the love I still have for her, with no place to go. So I have to give it to you all. I have to let it out into the world, to tell you about her laugh, her wisdom, her boundless, fierce compassion. She is gone, and I am shattered. But I am also the monument she spent a lifetime building. Every kindness I show, every story I tell, every life I touch, will be her legacy. I will carry you forward, Grandma. I will not let the world forget your song.
